purpose: How an installing GPS-tracking reseller converts a signed fleet deal into a fully working, lawful and disclosed deployment: selecting OBD, hardwired or battery asset devices per unit, designing installs that balance concealment against serviceability, provisioning the platform account with geofences, alerts and reports shaped to the fleet's actual workflow, onboarding drivers with the required disclosure, and proving every unit works before acceptance starts the subscription clock.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors

this is an own-install vertical: the reseller who installs the tracker also operates the monthly subscription afterward, so every install and configuration choice is judged by whether the unit stays supportable and the account stays adopted for years, not by whether the install day ends on time
all tracking deployed here is owner- or employer-authorized and disclosed to affected drivers; requests to covertly track private individuals are refused at intake, before any device is quoted

ELD/hours-of-service mandates and telematics- or employee-privacy rules vary by jurisdiction and fleet type, so this KB names obligation classes and flags verify-current-rules-in-your-jurisdiction instead of asserting local specifics
hardware costs, subscription rates and install times appear only as mechanisms and qualitative bands computed from each deal's own facts, never as invented figures stated as fact
the fleet, its parking pattern and its cellular environment are as found at intake; a material fleet change (new vehicle classes, new territory, new take-home policy) re-opens the affected decisions
exclusions: which fleets to target, platform-reseller versus white-label economics, hardware-plus-subscription offer design and ROI-based selling - that is KB1 (Fleet-Tracking Market & Reseller Economics) territory; this KB receives a signed deal with a unit list and hands back nothing about pricing

running the recurring service after acceptance - per-unit MRR management, device-health and data-quality monitoring in operation, renewals and contract hygiene, in-account expansion (more vehicles, assets, dashcams, maintenance modules), churn signals and support economics at unit scale - that is KB3 (Tracking Subscriptions & Fleet-Account Growth) territory; this KB delivers it a verified fleet, a documentation pack and a trained admin
covert tracking of private individuals in any form - a spouse's, ex-partner's or acquaintance's vehicle, or an employee's personal car - such requests are refused at intake, not merely descoped
hiding tracking from the fleet's own employees: concealment decisions here defend against thieves and tampering, never against the disclosed workforce

jurisdiction-specific legal advice on ELD/hours-of-service, employee monitoring consent, or telematics data privacy - obligation classes are named and flagged verify-locally, never asserted as the local rule
stated per-unit hardware prices, monthly subscription figures or per-install labor quotes - economics appear only as mechanisms and qualitative bands
vehicle repair, diagnostics work and electrical trades beyond what the tracker install itself requires; dashcam and video-telematics systems except as an expansion opportunity noted for KB3

competency_questions.question: What must the intake survey capture about a fleet before any tracking hardware is ordered?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INSTALL_INTAKE_SURVEY lists the per-unit facts (type, power, port, parking pattern, duty cycle) and the fleet-level facts (who dispatches, who reads reports, which questions the owner wants answered) that downstream decisions read from

competency_questions.question: When is a tracking job lawful to take, and how is a covert-tracking request recognized and refused?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LAWFUL_USE_GATE states the owner/employer-authorization test, the driver-disclosure requirement, the refusal line for tracking private individuals, and the screening questions that unmask a fleet-shaped covert request

competency_questions.question: Which regulation classes can touch a fleet-tracking rollout, and how are they handled without giving legal advice?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REGULATORY_FLAG_MAP names the ELD/hours-of-service and telematics/employee-privacy obligation classes, states that a GPS tracker is not an ELD absent named certification, and routes every specific to verify-current-rules-in-jurisdiction

competency_questions.question: Which device class - OBD plug-in, hardwired, or battery asset tracker - fits each unit class in a mixed fleet, and what disqualifies a class?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: USE_CASE_DEVICE_MATRIX gives the per-class mapping with reasons, and OBD_DEVICE_SELECTION and ASSET_TRACKER_SELECTION supply the disqualifiers (occupied or non-standard ports, unplug exposure, no vehicle power, battery-life budget)

competency_questions.question: How is a hardwired install designed on a modern vehicle, including power, ignition sensing and mounting?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: HARDWIRED_INSTALL_DESIGN covers constant-power and ignition-source discovery on multiplexed vehicles, virtual-ignition fallbacks, fused tap points, and mounting that preserves GPS sky view while avoiding airbag and CAN circuits

competency_questions.question: How deep should a tracker be concealed, and against whom is concealment legitimate?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CONCEALMENT_SERVICEABILITY_TRADEOFF states the shallowest-mount-that-meets-documented-risk rule, the service and antenna costs of hiding, and the boundary that concealment targets thieves and tamperers, never the disclosed workforce

competency_questions.question: How is cellular coverage risk assessed for a fleet's operating area, and what does out-of-coverage buffering do to the data the customer sees?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NETWORK_COVERAGE_CHECK describes per-area carrier qualification, store-and-forward buffering and its teleporting-track artifact, network-sunset exposure, and why coverage is checked before a SKU is committed fleet-wide

competency_questions.question: How should the platform account, groups, naming and user roles be structured to mirror how the fleet actually runs?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PLATFORM_ACCOUNT_PROVISIONING covers group hierarchy matching crews or branches, a naming convention fixed before first pairing, least-privilege roles per job function, and account-wide time zone and business-hours settings

competency_questions.question: How are geofences, alerts and reports configured to the fleet's workflow without creating sprawl or alert fatigue?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GEOFENCE_ARCHITECTURE ties every fence to a consuming report or alert, ALERT_TUNING requires a named acting recipient per alert and start-few-tune-up thresholds, and REPORT_WORKFLOW_MAPPING maps each scheduled report to a real fleet decision and decision-maker

competency_questions.question: How is driver disclosure and onboarding run so the rollout does not produce sabotage, grievances or turnover?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: DRIVER_DISCLOSURE_ONBOARDING specifies the written policy content, signed acknowledgment before go-live, honest framing of purposes, a dispute path, and union or works-council consultation flagged for jurisdiction verification

competency_questions.question: What must the per-unit verification test prove before the installer leaves the vehicle?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PER_UNIT_VERIFICATION_TEST requires live position at the install location, identity match against the pairing manifest, ignition events where supported, a coherent test-drive track, and one live-fired key alert, recorded per unit

competency_questions.question: How is a non-reporting unit triaged at install time, and when does diagnosis stop in favor of a swap?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TROUBLE_TRIAGE_AT_INSTALL gives the power / GPS / cellular three-bucket split with field discriminators, the human unplug bucket, and the one-attempt-per-bucket-then-swap policy

competency_questions.question: What do the documentation pack and the fleet acceptance gate contain before the account is handed to recurring operations?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INSTALL_DOCUMENTATION_PACK lists the per-unit record (device ID, SIM, asset identity, photographed mount and tap points, verification result) and FLEETWIDE_ACCEPTANCE_GATE lists the sign-off conditions including the intake questions demonstrated answered on live data

competency_questions.question: How is install day planned so vehicle downtime stays acceptable and absent vehicles do not collapse the batch?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INSTALL_SCHEDULING_LOGISTICS covers batching by yard and device class, realistic per-class bay times, pre-staged activated and labeled devices, and the fallback plan for vehicles missing from the yard

glossary.definition: The standardized diagnostic connector in light vehicles that plug-in trackers draw power and (sometimes) vehicle data from; heavy trucks use different connectors, commonly a 9-pin round deutsch style on J1939 wiring, so a consumer OBD-II tracker does not simply plug into a highway tractor.

A tracker installed on a three-wire scheme - constant battery power, an ignition-state sense, and ground - mounted out of casual reach; slower to install than a plug-in but permanent, tamper-resistant and invisible to the port.

A self-powered tracker for unpowered assets (trailers, containers, compressors, attachments) that reports on a sparse schedule to stretch a non-rechargeable battery across years; its whole design is a budget of fixes-per-day against battery life.

How often a device reports a position; faster pings give finer tracks and quicker alerts but spend battery on asset trackers and data allowance everywhere, so the rate is chosen per use case, not maximized.

Detecting engine on/off without a clean switched wire, using voltage-threshold sensing (charging voltage rise) or accelerometer motion; the standard fallback on modern multiplexed vehicles where a 'switched' circuit may stay live or wake on its own.
A virtual boundary drawn in the platform - radius or polygon - whose entry and exit events feed alerts and visit reports; useful exactly in proportion to whether some report or alert consumes it.

Device behavior out of cellular coverage: positions are logged internally and uploaded in a burst when coverage returns, which makes the track appear to jump or teleport; a data artifact to explain to the fleet admin, not a device fault.

The single-source-of-truth table binding each device ID and SIM to one asset's VIN or serial, its human-readable unit name, and its odometer or hour-meter baseline; every label on install day is printed from it.

The condition where over-alerting trains recipients to delete or mute everything, including the alert that mattered; the design counter is that every configured alert has a named recipient who will act on it.

A regulated device class that records driving hours for fleets subject to hours-of-service mandates; a distinct certification regime from ordinary GPS tracking, so no tracker is presented as an ELD unless the specific device-and-platform combination is verifiably certified in the customer's jurisdiction.

source_registry.description: heuristic prior estimates for tracker_installation_and_platform_onboarding work units in absence of supplied datasets
source_registry.citation_or_locator: heuristic prior; no external dataset supplied

nodes.definition: Capture, before any hardware is ordered, the facts every downstream choice reads from: a unit-by-unit fleet list (year, make and model or equipment type, VIN or serial, powered versus unpowered, diagnostic-port type on trucks), duty cycles and the overnight parking pattern (yard-parked, take-home, scattered across job sites), who dispatches and who will read reports, the operational questions the owner actually wants answered (where were my crews, whose hours do I bill, which trailer sits idle), and the physical realities of install day (yard hours, bay or parking-lot work, which units rotate through town). One intake sheet feeds the device matrix, the platform structure, the schedule and the disclosure rollout; a vehicle count scribbled on a quote feeds none of them.

included: per-unit fleet list with power and port facts
the owner's target questions and report readers

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a downstream rework is traced to a missing or wrong intake fact, or a fleet type appears that the sheet's fields do not describe

pros.claim: A per-unit intake sheet turns 'track my trucks' into a buildable plan before money is spent on the wrong hardware
pros.example: intake reveals that half an excavation outfit's 'trucks' are unpowered tilt trailers, changing the order from OBD plugs to battery asset trackers before anything ships

cons.claim: A thorough intake costs owner time before any visible progress, which strains small-fleet patience
cons.example: a three-crew plumbing outfit balks at listing VINs and overnight parking when they expected trackers in the mail the same week

failure_modes: ordering devices off a vehicle count instead of a unit list and eating the exchange
missing take-home vehicles that change the disclosure and off-hours privacy posture
assuming every unit parks in one yard when crews scatter trucks across home driveways
acceptance_tests: every unit on the order carries type, power source, port type where relevant, parking pattern and duty notes, and the owner's target questions are written down with a named reader per question
revisit_triggers: units are added, sold or re-assigned after intake
the fleet's dispatch, billing or take-home policy changes
an install or onboarding decision is traced to a fact intake failed to capture

nodes.definition: Enforce the bright line every job passes before quoting or installing: trackers go only on vehicles and assets the customer owns or controls as employer or lessor, employees who drive tracked vehicles are told, and requests to covertly track a private individual - a spouse, an ex-partner, a 'friend just checking' on someone's car - are refused at intake regardless of the revenue attached. The gate also sets the posture for gray requests: a take-home company vehicle can be tracked but pulls in off-hours privacy questions that must be disclosed and jurisdiction-checked, and 'do not tell the drivers' converts a legitimate fleet job into a covert-surveillance request this business does not perform. Staff carry a short, practiced refusal script so the line holds under sales pressure and sympathy stories alike.

included: refusal line and script for covert-individual requests
excluded: jurisdiction-specific legal conclusions - flagged for verification

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a refused or slipped-through case shows the screening questions missing a disguise pattern, or regulator guidance redraws the employee-tracking line

pros.claim: A stated refusal line keeps the business from becoming an instrument of stalking and out of the legal exposure covert tracking carries
pros.example: a walk-in wanting a magnetic tracker 'for my wife's car' gets a calm scripted refusal instead of an improvised maybe from whoever answers the counter

cons.claim: The gate costs real revenue and produces awkward conversations with customers who feel entitled to a yes
cons.example: a fleet owner walks after being told his drivers must be notified before the trackers go live

failure_modes: treating 'it is my company truck' as ending the inquiry when the request is really about following one person off-hours
letting an urgent install skip the authorization question
counter staff without the script improvising exceptions for sympathetic stories
acceptance_tests: ownership or employer/lessor authority is confirmed per asset before quote, every driver-notification obligation is identified, and refused covert requests are logged with the script used
revisit_triggers: a customer's story changes between quote and install day
an installed account asks for driver visibility or disclosure to be quietly turned off
guidance on employee-tracking consent changes in a served jurisdiction

nodes.definition: Maintain the map of regulation classes that can touch a tracking rollout, without playing counsel: ELD/hours-of-service mandates that bind certain commercial fleet and vehicle classes but not others; telematics- and employee-privacy rules that vary by jurisdiction (consent and notification requirements, off-hours limits, union or works-council consultation duties); and data-retention questions the fleet may face. The discipline is classify-and-flag: identify which classes plausibly apply to this fleet's type, size and operating territory, state plainly that a GPS tracker is not an ELD unless the specific device-and-platform combination is certified for that mandate, and route every 'does the law require or allow X here' to verification of current rules in the customer's jurisdiction before anything is promised in writing.

included: obligation-class identification per fleet type and territory
excluded: asserting any jurisdiction's current rule as fact
compliance consulting as a service line

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a compliance question from a live deal falls outside the mapped classes, or a served jurisdiction's telematics rules are reported revised

pros.claim: Naming the obligation class early keeps the sale honest and the install out of compliance trouble it cannot see
pros.example: catching that a mixed fleet's two heavy trucks may sit under hours-of-service rules the light-duty vans do not, before the customer assumes one system covers all compliance

cons.claim: Flag-and-verify adds friction and can read as evasive to a customer who wants a straight yes
cons.example: an owner irritated that 'can I ditch paper logs with this' earns 'that depends on certification and your fleet class - verify before relying on it'

failure_modes: selling ordinary GPS tracking as ELD or hours-of-service compliance
assuming one jurisdiction's employee-notification rule travels to the next
missing fleet-type boundaries (rented equipment, cross-border lanes) that change which classes apply
acceptance_tests: each engagement lists the regulation classes plausibly in play, every class carries a verify-current-rules-in-jurisdiction flag rather than an asserted specific, and no compliance capability is claimed without named certification
revisit_triggers: the fleet's type, territory or vehicle mix changes
a mandate or privacy rule relevant to a served fleet class is reported changed

nodes.definition: Decide, per unit class in the fleet, which device family does the job and record the reason: OBD plug-ins for light vehicles where install speed, self-install or easy transfer matter and the port is free; hardwired units where permanence, tamper resistance, true ignition state or an out-of-reach mount matter, and for heavy trucks whose diagnostic connectors and electrics are not consumer OBD-II; battery asset trackers for unpowered trailers, containers and equipment, trading ping rate against a multi-year battery; wired asset trackers where the equipment has its own power. The written reason per class matters because the wrong family is the most expensive early mistake in this trade: it surfaces as a fleet-wide re-order and re-install, not as a settings change.

included: per-unit-class device family decision with recorded reason
the cost asymmetry of a wrong family choice
excluded: specific SKU procurement and vendor negotiation
install technique per family (its own nodes)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a family-level misfit shows up in triage or early operations, or a new device family (solar asset units, dual-mode) changes the available choices

pros.claim: Mapping device class to use case per unit prevents the one-device-fits-all order that mixed fleets punish
pros.example: a rental yard gets battery asset trackers on tilt trailers, hardwired units in the dually pickups and nothing OBD, because every OBD port in the yard is used by the shop's scan tool weekly

cons.claim: A per-class matrix multiplies SKUs to stock, train on and support
cons.example: carrying three device families for one twelve-unit landscaping fleet means three install procedures and three failure profiles for the same monthly revenue

failure_modes: shipping OBD plug-ins to a fleet of heavy tractors with 9-pin connectors
putting powered trackers on assets that sit unpowered for months and die reporting nothing
choosing by hardware margin instead of by use case and eating the re-install
acceptance_tests: every unit class in the fleet maps to exactly one device family with a written reason, and no class is mapped to a family its power source or connector cannot support
revisit_triggers: triage finds a repeated failure class tied to one family choice
the fleet adds a unit class the matrix has not mapped
a device family's network generation faces sunset in the operating area

nodes.definition: Qualify OBD plug-and-play trackers for the subset of the fleet they genuinely fit: light vehicles with a standard OBD-II port, customers who value fast install, self-install or easy transfer between vehicles, and pilots that must show value before the fleet commits to hardwiring. The expertise lives in the limits: the port is occupied (colliding with insurance dongles and the shop's scan tool), the device is visible and takes one second to unplug - so its security posture rests on disclosure plus unplug alerting, not on hiding; some vehicles cut or keep port power in ways that change reporting behavior; and heavy trucks are not OBD-II, their 9-pin deutsch-style connectors need an adapter harness or a hardwired unit instead.

excluded: reading or interpreting vehicle diagnostic data as a service

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: field unplug rates or port-conflict reports shift the family's fit boundary, or vehicle makers change port power behavior in common fleet models

pros.claim: Minutes-per-unit install and clean self-install make OBD the lowest-friction entry for light fleets and pilots
pros.example: a courier fleet self-installs twenty units mailed with one-page instructions, and the reseller verifies them remotely the same afternoon

cons.claim: One-second removal makes the OBD unit the first casualty of a resentful rollout or a driver with something to hide
cons.example: the van whose tracker goes offline every Friday afternoon turns out to have a driver who unplugs it before side jobs

failure_modes: shipping OBD units to trucks whose ports are non-standard or already occupied
relying on concealment for a device that sits in plain sight under the column
skipping unplug alerting and losing the only tamper defense the family has
acceptance_tests: every OBD-assigned vehicle has a confirmed free standard port, and unplug or power-loss alerting is configured for the family before go-live
revisit_triggers: unplug events cluster on specific vehicles or shifts
the customer's shop reports port conflicts with diagnostic work

nodes.definition: Design the hardwired install per vehicle model before touching the first unit: find constant battery power and a true ignition-state source - increasingly non-trivial on multiplexed vehicles where a nominally switched circuit stays live or wakes on its own, which is when voltage-threshold or accelerometer-based virtual ignition takes over; choose a fused tap point over a bare splice; pick a mount that balances GPS sky view, distance from electrical noise, and the concealment decision; and stay clear of airbag circuits, CAN wiring an installer has no business splicing, and anything that invites a warranty dispute with the customer's dealer. The design is written once per vehicle model in the fleet and reused across the batch, so the first truck of each model is the slow, careful one.

included: per-model power, ignition and ground plan
mount location balancing antenna, noise and concealment
excluded: the workmanship execution standard (its own node)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a designed model shows ignition-sense or power faults in verification, or vehicle-electronics changes invalidate a standard tap point

pros.claim: A per-model design sheet turns a fleet hardwire batch into repetition instead of twenty explorations
pros.example: after one careful hour on the first of nine identical service vans, the remaining eight each take a fraction of that using the same tap points and mount

cons.claim: Modern vehicle electronics keep invalidating yesterday's ignition-wire knowledge
cons.example: a current-year pickup's 'ignition' circuit wakes for telematics updates at 3am, logging ghost trips until the design flips to voltage-sense virtual ignition

failure_modes: tapping a circuit that wakes randomly and generating ghost ignition events
an unfused tap that later shorts and takes a vehicle circuit with it
mounting under enough steel that the GPS fix degrades to uselessness
acceptance_tests: each vehicle model in the batch has a written design naming power, ignition (real or virtual), ground, mount location and fuse protection, proven on the first unit of that model before the batch proceeds
revisit_triggers: ghost trips or missed ignition events appear on a designed model
a new vehicle model enters the fleet without a design sheet

nodes.definition: Select and configure trackers for unpowered assets - trailers, containers, compressors, attachments, machines that sit for weeks: set the ping schedule as a spent budget (a few fixes a day buys years of battery; every extra fix and every cold month draws it down), specify a faster in-motion rate and a recovery mode that ramps reporting when the asset moves outside expectation, choose mounting that gives the antenna sky view on a steel machine while surviving pressure washing and branch strikes, and match motion-wake sensitivity to how the asset actually moves so a rail-yard bump does not burn a month of battery in false wakes. Where the asset has its own power (reefer units, some heavy equipment), a wired asset tracker removes the battery budget entirely and is preferred.

included: mounting for sky view and abuse survival
excluded: theft investigation and recovery operations after a loss (KB3 operations)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: observed battery life diverges from the configured band, or a customer's loss event shows the recovery mode mismatched to their expectation

pros.claim: A sparse-ping asset tracker finally makes the unpowered majority of many fleets visible at all
pros.example: a rental yard learns which of its forty tilt trailers have not moved in ninety days, an answer no powered-vehicle system could give

cons.claim: Sparse pings mean the platform's picture of an asset is hours or a day old, which surprises customers trained by live vehicle maps
cons.example: an owner watching a stolen trailer's dot expects live pursuit and gets a last-known fix from 6am plus a recovery-mode wait

failure_modes: configuring vehicle-style ping rates and killing the battery inside months
mounting under a steel deck so the unit works on the bench and fails in the field
motion-wake set so sensitive that yard handling drains the battery in false alarms
acceptance_tests: each asset class has a written ping schedule with an expected battery-life band, and the mount spec names sky-view orientation and abuse protection
revisit_triggers: battery drain runs ahead of the design band
the customer's recovery expectations conflict with the configured schedule

nodes.definition: Qualify the cellular reality the fleet will live in before a SKU is committed fleet-wide: which carriers actually hold in the yards, rural job sites, underground garages and cross-border lanes the intake mapped; what the chosen device does out of coverage - store-and-forward buffering that later uploads a burst of stale fixes, making tracks appear to teleport unless the admin has been told to expect it; whether the device generation rides a network technology facing sunset in the operating region, which converts a working fleet into paperweights on a carrier's schedule, not the reseller's; and roaming and SIM policy for fleets that cross borders. Coverage failures masquerade as device failures, and at fleet scale that misdiagnosis burns trust faster than any single bad unit.

included: buffering behavior and its data artifacts
network-sunset exposure of a device generation

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: field data contradicts a qualified area's coverage note, or a sunset announcement or new roaming policy touches the deployed base

pros.claim: Checking coverage per operating area before committing hardware prevents the fleet-wide swap that a sunset or dead-zone discovery forces later
pros.example: a logging fleet's laydown yards sit in a coverage hole one carrier's map admits and another's does not; the SIM choice follows the honest map, not the cheaper plan

cons.claim: Carrier coverage maps flatter themselves, so real qualification needs field checks that cost time
cons.example: a map shows solid coverage at a quarry whose pit floor gets nothing; only the site walk with a test unit finds it

failure_modes: committing a single-carrier SKU fleet-wide off a marketing coverage map
not warning the admin about buffering, so the first teleporting track becomes a support crisis of confidence
selling remaining stock of a device generation into a region where its network is being retired
acceptance_tests: each operating area on the intake sheet has a coverage note naming carrier(s) qualified, known dead zones, and the buffering behavior to expect, and no committed SKU rides a network flagged for sunset in that region
revisit_triggers: buffered or missing tracks cluster in an area marked as covered
a carrier announces a technology sunset touching deployed device generations

nodes.definition: Decide, per install class, how hidden the device should be - and against whom. Concealment defends high-value assets against theft-ring removal and defeats casual tampering, but every layer of hiding costs service time later (a panel teardown per battery swap or fault call), risks burying the GPS antenna under metal, and never legitimately means hiding tracking from the fleet's own disclosed drivers: the workforce knows the vehicles are tracked even where a unit's exact mounting spot is not advertised. The working rule is the shallowest mount that meets the documented tamper and theft risk for that asset class, with the exact location photographed into the install record so future service is a five-minute panel pop instead of archaeology.

included: per-class concealment depth decision against documented risk
service-cost and antenna consequences of hiding
excluded: covert tracking of any person (refused at LAWFUL_USE_GATE)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: tamper/theft outcomes or service-time data show a class's concealment depth miscalibrated in either direction

pros.claim: Concealment calibrated to documented risk protects exactly the assets thieves actually strip
pros.example: a skid steer that works unattended lots gets its tracker buried behind the boom harness where a thief with a knife and five minutes will not find it, while the yard pickups keep serviceable under-dash mounts

cons.claim: Every hidden mount is a future labor bill and a triage handicap
cons.example: a battery swap that should take minutes takes an hour of interior panel work because the original installer hid the unit deep and photographed nothing

failure_modes: hiding so deep the antenna loses sky view and the unit reports garbage
defaulting every install to maximum concealment because it feels professional
letting a customer reframe concealment as hiding the program from drivers
acceptance_tests: each install class records a concealment depth with the documented risk that justifies it, and every concealed mount has a location photo in the install record
revisit_triggers: a tamper or theft event defeats the chosen depth
service calls on a class run long because of its concealment choice

nodes.definition: Hold every install to fixed standards that do not flex with the schedule: every power tap fused (inline fuse or a proper fuse-tap, never insulation-displacement taps on circuits that matter), wiring loomed and dressed so it cannot chafe, drop into pedal travel, or announce itself as a rattle; no contact with airbag, safety-restraint or CAN circuits; connectors weatherproofed on assets that live outdoors; adhesives and mounts rated for dash heat and equipment vibration; and a photo of the finished mount and tap points taken before panels close. The standard exists because the failure it prevents - an electrical fault the customer attributes to the tracker installer, sometimes correctly - costs more in warranty labor and reputation than every minute the standard adds across a batch.

included: fusing, dressing, routing and weatherproofing standards

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an electrical fault traces to an install, or a deviation pattern appears in spot checks

pros.claim: A non-negotiable workmanship floor makes install quality independent of which tech and which schedule pressure
pros.example: two years on, a service call finds every unit in the fleet fused and loomed the same way, so the fault hunt starts from a known baseline instead of twenty personal styles

cons.claim: The standard's minutes-per-unit are real and tempting to shave on a big batch
cons.example: loom, fuse and photo add measurable time across thirty vans, and a crew behind schedule will quietly drop the photo first

failure_modes: an unfused tap shorting and taking out a vehicle circuit with the customer's trust
wiring dressed into pedal travel or an airbag path
panels closed with no photo, converting every future service call into exploration
acceptance_tests: spot-check of any completed unit finds fused taps, loomed and secured wiring clear of no-go zones, weatherproofing on exposed connectors, and a stored photo of mount and tap points
revisit_triggers: verification or service finds a workmanship deviation pattern
a new vehicle or asset class needs a standard the checklist lacks

nodes.definition: Plan install days around the fleet's operating reality, because downtime is the customer's cost center: batch by yard and by device class; book windows when vehicles are actually parked (nights, weekends, early mornings - whatever the parking pattern from intake says); set realistic per-unit bay times by class (an OBD unit in minutes, a hardwire in the better part of an hour, assets varying with access); stage devices pre-activated, labeled per the pairing manifest and sorted per vehicle before crews arrive; and hold a fallback for the certainty that some listed vehicles will be absent - on a job, in the shop, or sold last month. A rollout that idles revenue vehicles teaches the customer the tracker costs money before it has saved any.

included: window selection from the parking pattern
excluded: the workmanship and verification content of each install
quoting install labor to the customer (mechanism territory, KB1)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: bay-time actuals or absent-vehicle rates from completed batches move the planning constants

pros.claim: Batching by parking window converts installs from fleet disruption into invisible overhead
pros.example: an HVAC fleet is done across two Saturday mornings in its own yard, and no crew loses a billable hour

cons.claim: Off-hours batching concentrates risk into windows with no slack
cons.example: one sick installer on the only Saturday the yard is full pushes the rollout a full week

failure_modes: scheduling against the vehicle list instead of the parking reality and finding half the yard empty
unstaged devices activated one at a time in the yard while trucks queue
no fallback when vehicles are absent, so the batch collapses instead of shrinking
acceptance_tests: the install plan names windows tied to the parking pattern, per-class bay-time budgets, a staging manifest, and a written fallback for absent vehicles
revisit_triggers: actual bay times run over budget by class
absent-vehicle rates break the batch plan twice running

nodes.definition: Build the platform account to mirror how the fleet actually runs before the first unit reports in: groups that match crews, branches or contracts so a supervisor sees their trucks and not everyone's; a naming convention fixed once, using the unit numbers the crew already shouts across the yard rather than VIN tails no human recognizes; user roles at least-privilege - dispatch sees live maps, payroll pulls reports, the owner sees everything, and nobody holds admin who does not need it; and account-wide time zone, odometer units and business-hours settings correct from day one, because every alert and report inherits them. Role design also carries the lawful-use posture into daily operation: access is scoped to legitimate business use, and a login whose pattern is one person watching one driver after hours is a misuse the structure should make visible rather than easy.

included: group hierarchy from the fleet's org
naming convention fixed before first pairing
excluded: geofence, alert and report content (their own nodes)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an org change, a visibility complaint, or a misuse signal shows the structure diverging from the fleet's reality

pros.claim: An account skeleton that mirrors the org makes every later screen self-explanatory to the fleet
pros.example: the north-branch dispatcher logs in for the first time and sees exactly the fourteen trucks she dispatches, named the way she already names them

cons.claim: Structure built from an org chart nobody updated fossilizes fast
cons.example: two crews merge in the spring and every group, alert route and scheduled report still reflects the winter org until someone rebuilds them

failure_modes: pairing units into a flat unstructured account and renaming everything after reports have shipped
everyone-is-admin provisioning that makes misuse and accidents equally easy
wrong account time zone silently skewing every after-hours alert and timecard report
acceptance_tests: before first pairing: groups mirror the fleet's stated org, the naming convention is written, each user holds the least role their job needs, and time zone and business hours are verified against intake
revisit_triggers: the fleet reorganizes crews, branches or contracts
a report reader cannot see, or can wrongly see, units outside their scope
access-pattern review suggests off-purpose individual monitoring

nodes.definition: Activate each device and bind it to the right asset before it reaches the vehicle: SIM and platform service confirmed live on the bench, device ID recorded against the unit's VIN or serial and its human name from the naming convention, odometer or hour-meter baseline entered where the platform supports it, and the pairing manifest treated as the single source of truth on install day - the box the installer carries is labeled with the vehicle it belongs to, printed from the manifest, not from memory. Mis-pairing is the quiet catastrophe of onboarding: every alert, report and timecard that follows attributes one vehicle's behavior to another, and it surfaces weeks later through an angry customer's payroll dispute instead of through the installer.

included: device-to-asset binding with VIN/serial and human name
excluded: renaming schemes after go-live (prevented, not managed)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an identity mismatch found at verification or in operation, or a manifest process gap that let a duplicate through

pros.claim: Bench-activated, manifest-labeled devices make install day a matching exercise instead of a provisioning exercise
pros.example: each van's box carries its unit number and the installer's only pairing duty is to confirm the label matches the vehicle in the bay

cons.claim: Bench activation spends subscription and battery clock before the fleet benefits
cons.example: thirty units activated Monday for a Saturday install run their first week of service life sitting in a bin

failure_modes: two boxes swapped in the yard, discovered a month later in a payroll dispute
activation attempted in the yard over one bar of signal while trucks queue
no odometer baseline entered, so maintenance-adjacent reports start from fiction
acceptance_tests: every device is confirmed reporting on the bench before install day, and the manifest binds device ID, SIM, VIN/serial, human name and baseline with no duplicates in any column
revisit_triggers: a verification identity check fails against the manifest
units are re-assigned between vehicles after go-live
the platform's pairing or naming model changes

nodes.definition: Design geofences as an encoding of the fleet's operational geography, not as decoration: the yard or yards first, because after-hours movement alerts and first-out/last-in visibility hang on them; then the recurring job sites and customer locations that billing or dispatch actually asks about; polygons where a radius would swallow the neighbors (the supply house across the street from a bar deserves a tight boundary); names that read in the fleet's own language so reports need no translation; and deliberate pruning - every fence no alert or report consumes is maintenance debt that rots the account. One-off sites get short-lived fences or none. The architecture serves the questions intake recorded, not the maximum the platform allows.

included: yard fences as the alert backbone
recurring-site fences tied to consuming reports
excluded: the alerts and reports that consume fences (their own nodes)
route planning and dispatch optimization products

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: fence-consumption review finds orphans, or a geography change (new yard, lost contract) invalidates the set

pros.claim: A small set of consumed, well-named fences turns raw tracks into answers the fleet recognizes
pros.example: the visit report reads 'Riverside jobsite 41 minutes' instead of a coordinate pair, and the office stops calling drivers to ask where they were

cons.claim: Geofence sprawl accumulates silently until the account is unmaintainable
cons.example: eighteen months of one-off jobsite fences nobody deleted turn the fence list into an archaeology layer no report consumes

failure_modes: a yard radius so generous the after-hours alert never fires because the truck 'never leaves'
fences named by whoever drew them, unreadable in reports
building a fence per historical jobsite because the import tool made it easy
acceptance_tests: every configured fence names a consuming alert or report, yard fences are polygon-verified against the actual property line, and names follow the account convention
revisit_triggers: the fleet gains or loses a yard or a recurring site
a fence-consuming report is retired

nodes.definition: Configure alerts under one rule: every alert has a named recipient who will act on it, or it does not exist. The backbone set for a typical fleet: after-hours movement from the yard fence routed to whoever genuinely answers at 2am (that is a theft signal, not a morning email); tamper, unplug and power-loss alerts - the OBD family's only real defense; low-battery warnings on asset trackers routed to whoever schedules battery swaps; and the driver-behavior family (speeding, harsh events, excessive idle) only at thresholds and volumes the fleet's management will actually work, because a speeding alert on every few miles over trains everyone to delete the folder unread. Behavior alerting also stays inside the disclosed program - alerts monitor what drivers were told is monitored. Start with few alerts and tune upward from observed events in the first weeks; never start from everything-on and hope to prune.

included: the backbone alert set and routing
excluded: coaching or disciplining drivers (the fleet's business)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: fired-alert outcomes from the first weeks (acted on, ignored, missed) move thresholds and routing

pros.claim: A small owned alert set gets acted on, which is the only thing an alert is for
pros.example: the 2am yard-exit alert goes to the owner's phone and the one time it fires in earnest, the trailer is recovered because someone actually woke up

cons.claim: Tuning to avoid fatigue means some real events go unalerted by design
cons.example: a modest speeding threshold means the van doing a little over the limit daily never pings anyone, and the owner learns of the habit from a complaint instead

failure_modes: everything-on defaults burying the one alert that mattered
alerts routed to a shared inbox nobody owns
behavior alerting expanded beyond what drivers were told is monitored
acceptance_tests: every configured alert names its recipient and the action expected, after-hours and tamper alerts are live-tested once, and behavior alerts match the disclosed policy
revisit_triggers: the week-one review finds a flooded or silent alert channel
a real event fails to alert or reaches someone who could not act
the disclosed policy changes what may be monitored

nodes.definition: Configure the small set of scheduled reports that answer the questions intake recorded, each delivered to the person who makes that decision: start/stop or timecard-style reports to whoever reconciles hours; idle and utilization summaries to whoever owns fuel or fleet-size decisions; geofence visit history to whoever proves service calls or bills time on site; an after-hours summary to the owner. The craft is subtraction - a fleet that receives ten reports reads none - and translation: names, units and groupings in the fleet's own vocabulary. Reports that back invoicing or payroll disputes are flagged evidence-grade: their credibility rests on verified pairing and correct account time settings, which is why they ship only after per-unit verification passes, and why a report contradicted by a paper timesheet triggers a data check before a confrontation.

excluded: building custom analytics beyond the platform's reports

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: read/unread patterns and dispute outcomes show which reports earn their place and which mislead

pros.claim: One report per real decision, to its decision-maker, is what converts tracking data into money the customer can point at
pros.example: the Friday hours report goes straight to the bookkeeper who reconciles timesheets, and the owner stops paying for hours no truck ever drove

cons.claim: Lean reporting leaves platform capability visibly unused, which some buyers read as underdelivery
cons.example: an owner who saw a demo of thirty report types asks why he only receives three, and the answer 'because you would read none of the others' has to be sold

failure_modes: shipping the platform's default report pack and calling onboarding done
reports delivered to whoever signed the contract instead of whoever makes the decision
an evidence-grade report shipped before verification, poisoning the first payroll reconciliation
acceptance_tests: every scheduled report names the intake question it answers and its reader, evidence-grade reports are gated behind verification, and no report ships without a named reader
revisit_triggers: a scheduled report goes unopened for consecutive cycles
a payroll or billing dispute questions a report's accuracy

nodes.definition: Run the workforce side of go-live as deliberately as the hardware side: a written tracking policy in plain language - what is collected, when, who sees it, what it is used for and what it is not used for; a signed acknowledgment from every affected driver before their unit goes live; a short session that frames the system honestly (billing proof, theft recovery, dispatch efficiency, defense against false claims - not a gotcha machine) with room for questions and pushback; and a named path for disputes about what the data shows. Where the workforce is unionized or a works council exists, consultation happens per that agreement before rollout - flagged for jurisdiction verification, since consultation duties differ. Disclosure done well is also operationally selfish: undisclosed or badly-framed rollouts come back as mysteriously unplugged devices, grievances and resignations, and the cheapest anti-sabotage measure this trade has is honesty.

excluded: jurisdiction-specific consent law conclusions (flagged, not asserted)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a grievance, sabotage cluster or consultation finding shows the disclosure process or policy content falling short

pros.claim: Disclosure-first rollouts protect the driver relationship the fleet depends on and the hardware the reseller just installed
pros.example: a delivery fleet's drivers, told plainly the data settles disputed overtime in their favor too, stop treating the tracker as the enemy - and the unplug rate that plagued a competitor's covert-style rollout never appears

cons.claim: Honest disclosure surfaces workforce conflict at rollout instead of letting it fester quietly
cons.example: two senior techs threaten to quit in the disclosure meeting itself, and the owner has to resolve in one week a trust question that covert rollouts defer for months

failure_modes: devices live before drivers are told, discovered via a dispatcher's slip
a policy that promises 'safety only' while management quietly reads location history for discipline
skipping union or works-council consultation where an agreement requires it
acceptance_tests: every affected driver has a signed acknowledgment dated before their unit went live, the policy states uses and non-uses in plain language, and any applicable collective-consultation step is documented or explicitly cleared
revisit_triggers: monitoring scope changes (new alert types, dashcams, off-hours visibility)
a grievance or dispute cites the policy
new hires join tracked vehicles

nodes.definition: Train the people who will live in the platform, sized to their actual day rather than to the feature list: the dispatcher's five-minute morning screen, the payroll clerk's weekly report pull, the owner's exception habit - look when an alert says look, not as a hobby; plus the small self-service set that prevents support calls (rename a unit, adjust a geofence, correctly silence an alert whose cause is fixed). The first week runs co-piloted: a scheduled fifteen-minute review of what alerts fired and what the reports said, which is exactly where mis-tuned thresholds, unread reports and wrong recipients surface while they are still cheap to fix. The measurable enemy is the account that logs in during week one and never again - installation is what the customer paid for, but adoption is what the subscription renews on.

included: the co-piloted first week and its review
excluded: long-run account health and renewal management (KB3)
training the fleet's drivers (disclosure covers their part)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: adoption telemetry (logins, report reads, alert responses) in the first month shows whether training landed

pros.claim: Role-sized training plus a co-piloted first week converts an installed system into a used one
pros.example: the week-one review catches that the idle report goes to a manager who cannot read it on his phone; one recipient change later, it is acted on weekly

cons.claim: Training and the first-week cadence are unbilled hours concentrated at the least profitable moment of the account
cons.example: three training sessions and two review calls land in the same month as the install labor, all against the first month's subscription

failure_modes: feature-tour training that impresses in the room and transfers nothing
no named admin on the fleet side, so the account is orphaned at handoff
skipping the week-one review and letting mis-tuned alerts calcify into ignore-everything habits
acceptance_tests: each platform user demonstrates their own routine unprompted, a named fleet-side admin exists, and the week-one review happened with its findings applied
revisit_triggers: login or report-read activity drops toward zero
the trained admin leaves the fleet

nodes.definition: Prove each unit works before its vehicle returns to service, and record the pass per unit: device online and showing a live position at the actual install location, not remembered from the bench an hour earlier; identity confirmed against the pairing manifest - the map pin moves when this vehicle moves; ignition-on and ignition-off events observed where the device class supports them; a short test drive producing a coherent track with sane speed and odometer movement; and the unit's key alert - unplug, tamper or movement, per class - fired once as a live end-to-end test that it reaches its recipient. The protocol exists because the alternative is discovering failures across a dispersed fleet after install day, where every fix costs a truck-chase to a job site instead of thirty seconds in the bay.

excluded: fault diagnosis when a check fails (TROUBLE_TRIAGE_AT_INSTALL)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: an escaped defect class (something operations catches that verification did not) adds a check to the protocol

pros.claim: Per-unit field verification catches at the bay, for seconds, what would otherwise cost a site visit per failure
pros.example: the test drive shows unit 12's pin parked while the truck moves - a bench-tested device whose antenna sits under the one bracket that blocks it - fixed in five minutes instead of found next week forty miles away

cons.claim: Full verification adds nontrivial minutes per unit, which multiplies painfully across a large batch
cons.example: on a thirty-van Saturday the test drives alone consume an installer-hour block the schedule must genuinely contain rather than wish away

failure_modes: bench-verified being treated as field-verified
skipping the identity check because the label 'must be' right
the alert round-trip untested until the first real theft finds the routing broken
acceptance_tests: a per-unit record shows live position at install location, manifest identity match, ignition events where supported, a coherent test-drive track, and one delivered key alert, before the vehicle returned to service
revisit_triggers: any unit's verification record is missing or failed at acceptance review
an in-operation fault appears on a unit that passed, questioning the protocol's coverage

nodes.definition: Diagnose non-reporting units at install time with the three-bucket split before swapping anything: no power (blown or wrong tap, dead port, loose connector), no GPS (buried antenna, steel overhead, the works-on-the-bench mount), no cellular (coverage hole, SIM or activation fault) - each with a fast field discriminator: LED codes, the platform's last-contact versus last-fix timestamps (contact without fix means cellular fine, GPS blind; neither means power or cellular), a meter on the tap, and the move-to-open-sky test. Include the human bucket: a disclosed-but-resentful driver's unplugged OBD unit is not a hardware fault and is handled through the fleet's management, not through a device swap. A swap policy bounds the time cost: one fix attempt per bucket, then swap the unit, label the pulled one for bench diagnosis, and never leave a vehicle unverified because the diagnosis got interesting.

included: labeling pulled units for bench work
excluded: in-operation device-health monitoring and RMA economics (KB3)
vehicle electrical repair beyond the tracker's own circuit

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: bench-versus-field bucket disagreement rates, or a new failure class the three buckets do not cover

pros.claim: The bucket split with discriminators keeps triage minutes-long and prevents the classic wrong fix
pros.example: last-contact fresh but last-fix stale says the 'dead' unit is a GPS-blind mount, so the fix is moving it a hand-width, not swapping hardware or blaming the carrier

cons.claim: The hard swap policy sacrifices root-cause knowledge in the field for schedule
cons.example: a unit that would have revealed a bad firmware batch gets swapped and binned in the yard's rhythm, and the pattern is only visible weeks later at the bench

failure_modes: swap-first triage that ships the same fault back out in a new box
treating driver unplugs as hardware failures and burning swaps on a management problem
diagnosing a coverage hole as a batch of bad devices
acceptance_tests: every non-reporting unit at install carries a triage record naming its bucket and discriminator evidence, and no vehicle left unverified due to open triage
revisit_triggers: a failure bucket's rate spikes across a batch
bench diagnosis of pulled units contradicts field bucket calls

nodes.definition: Assemble the per-unit record that makes every later touch cheap: device ID and SIM, asset identity (VIN or serial plus human name), install date and installer, device class and configuration notes, mount location and fuse-tap points photographed before the panels closed, and the verification result with its date. Rolled up across the fleet with the account structure, disclosure records and exception list, the pack becomes the handoff artifact recurring operations inherits: it is the difference between 'unit 14 stopped reporting' meaning a five-minute panel pop by any tech, and meaning a teardown expedition that only the original installer - who left last spring - could have shortened.

included: fleet-level rollup as the operations handoff

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: service-call friction traced to missing record fields, or an operations request that extends the pack's schema

pros.claim: Photographed mounts and tap points convert future service from exploration into procedure
pros.example: a tech who has never seen the truck opens the record, sees the unit behind the left kick panel tapped at fuse F23, and finishes the swap inside the customer's coffee break

cons.claim: Documentation is the first casualty of a running-late install day and its absence is invisible until needed
cons.example: the batch's last five vans have no photos because the crew was chasing daylight, and nobody notices until a warranty call eighteen months later

failure_modes: records living in an installer's phone gallery instead of the account file
photos taken after panels closed, showing nothing useful
the rollup never delivered, so operations re-derives fleet facts by calling the customer
acceptance_tests: a randomly sampled unit's record contains all fields including pre-close photos and verification result, and the fleet rollup is filed where operations reads it
revisit_triggers: a service call finds a record missing or wrong
operations requests fields the pack does not carry

nodes.definition: Close onboarding with an explicit fleet-level acceptance instead of a fade-out: every unit verified or on a dated exception list with a fix plan; disclosure acknowledgments complete; the admin trained with the week-one review scheduled; the documentation pack delivered; and - the step that sells the renewal before the first invoice - each of the owner's intake questions demonstrated answered on their own live data, walking them through 'whose hours bill' on last Tuesday's actual tracks. A signature closes the gate, starts the subscription clock, and hands the account to recurring operations. The gate defends both sides: the customer knows exactly what done meant, and the reseller holds an artifact that separates install defects from the later service issues KB3 will manage.

included: signature, subscription start and operations handoff
excluded: everything after handoff - renewals, expansion, churn management (KB3)
re-negotiating scope or price at signature (KB1)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: acceptance disputes or handoff friction reveal a missing gate condition, or operations' early-fault data shows the gate passing defects

pros.claim: A demonstrated-on-your-own-data acceptance converts the customer's leap of faith into observed value at the exact moment the subscription begins
pros.example: the owner watches his own Tuesday data settle a job-hours question he has argued about for years, and the monthly fee stops being an expense in his mind before the first invoice lands

cons.claim: A formal gate hands the customer a lever to withhold acceptance over items outside the install's scope
cons.example: signature stalls for three weeks over a feature request the platform never promised, while the unbilled subscription clock question festers

failure_modes: the fade-out non-ending, where nobody can later say when onboarding ended and support began
accepting with an exception list that has no dates or owners and therefore never shrinks
skipping the live-data demonstration and leaving the value undemonstrated until renewal
acceptance_tests: the signed acceptance lists all-units-verified-or-excepted with dates and owners, disclosure and training confirmations, pack delivery, and the intake questions demonstrated on live data
revisit_triggers: an exception list item passes its fix date
operations disputes whether an early fault predates acceptance
the acceptance demonstration fails on any intake question

edges.why_related: the device matrix maps unit classes the intake sheet enumerated; without per-unit power and port facts there is nothing to map
groups, naming and roles are built from the org, readers and unit names intake recorded
coverage is qualified per operating area, and the operating areas come from intake's yards, sites and lanes
the disclosure rollout operationalizes the notification obligation the lawful-use gate established for this fleet
consultation and consent steps in the disclosure plan follow the obligation classes the map flagged for this fleet type and territory
OBD qualification details the plug-in branch of the family decision the matrix made per unit class
hardwire design work begins only for the unit classes the matrix assigned to the hardwired family
asset-tracker configuration serves the unpowered classes the matrix identified from intake's power facts
concealment depth is chosen among the mount options the per-model design established as electrically and antenna-wise viable
the workmanship standard executes the tap points and routes the per-model design specified
fences are drawn inside the account's group structure and naming convention, which must exist first
the backbone after-hours and site alerts consume yard and site fences; alert design starts from which fences exist
reports group and name units per the account structure; readers get scoped by the role design
the verification identity check tests the field install against the pairing manifest, which must exist and be authoritative first
verification proves the physical install the standard governed; a unit cannot pass verification before it is installed to standard
fleet acceptance aggregates per-unit verification passes; the gate's first condition is built from these records
acceptance requires a trained named admin and a scheduled week-one review, which training produces
pack delivery is an acceptance condition; the gate cannot close on undocumented installs
concealment may target thieves and tamperers only; hiding the program from the disclosed workforce is outside the lawful posture no matter the mounting logic
edges.risk_of_conflict: a customer reframes anti-theft concealment as keeping drivers in the dark

edges.why_related: role and access design must scope visibility to legitimate business use, so the account structure cannot enable covert individual monitoring the gate refused
edges.risk_of_conflict: an owner demands a private login to watch one employee outside the disclosed program

edges.why_related: driver-behavior alerting sits under jurisdiction-specific employee-monitoring classes, so behavior alerts stay within flagged-and-disclosed bounds pending verification
edges.risk_of_conflict: behavior alerting expands past what the jurisdictional check and the disclosed policy cover

edges.why_related: no report may be framed as hours-of-service or ELD compliance output unless the device-platform certification for that mandate is verified
edges.risk_of_conflict: a timecard-style report drifts into being sold as a compliance log

edges.why_related: asset trackers live where assets sit - laydown yards, rural sites - so the coverage qualification bounds which device generations and carriers the asset classes may use
edges.risk_of_conflict: an otherwise ideal asset device rides a network absent exactly where the assets park

edges.why_related: every layer of concealment slows the physical half of triage and every future service touch
edges.resolution_rule: serviceability wins absent a documented tamper or theft risk for that asset class; where concealment is justified, the photographed mount record must cap triage cost, and a concealed mount without its photo is a standards violation

edges.why_related: batch throughput pressure pushes crews to shave exactly the fusing, dressing and photo minutes the standard mandates
edges.resolution_rule: the workmanship standard wins unconditionally; the batch shrinks or gains a day, and any unit that skipped the standard is reopened and brought to it before verification

edges.why_related: the schedule's worst hour is exactly when skipping test drives and alert round-trips looks cheapest
edges.resolution_rule: no vehicle returns to service unverified; if the window closes, the remaining units carry to the fallback window rather than leaving as unverified installs

edges.why_related: the families compete for the same light vehicles: OBD's speed and self-install against hardwire's permanence, ignition truth and tamper resistance
edges.resolution_rule: hardwired wins where unplug exposure, port conflicts, heavy-truck connectors or ignition-truth requirements exist; OBD wins for pilots, self-install customers and high-churn rental vehicles, and then mandatory unplug alerting is part of the choice

edges.why_related: a badly-run disclosure produces the resentful-unplug failure class that triage must then separate from genuine hardware faults
an over-alerted first week trains the admin to ignore the platform, and no amount of later training recovers an audience taught that alerts mean nothing
photographed mounts and tap points convert the physical half of any later no-report call from teardown into a short procedure
known dead zones and expected buffering pre-classify a whole family of no-report symptoms, keeping them out of the hardware buckets
batch windows are chosen from the parking pattern and yard hours intake recorded, so scheduling follows intake in build order
staging happens against the schedule: bench-activated, manifest-labeled boxes are sorted per vehicle before crews arrive at the yard
drivers are notified before their units go live, so acknowledgment collection precedes activation going hot in the fleet
verification failures route straight into triage while the installer and vehicle are still in the same place
triage outcomes either clear units for acceptance or populate the dated exception list the gate requires
recurring verification failures rewrite the standard - a mount spot that keeps burying GPS gets banned, a tap that keeps blowing gets a new fuse spec
the week-one co-review returns fired-alert reality - flooded, silent, misrouted - to the thresholds and recipients
acceptance misses and demonstration failures reveal intake blind spots that update the survey template for the next fleet
both translate the fleet's operational geography and questions into platform configuration, and both fail the same way - by sprawl that nobody consumes

conflict_axes.name: concealment_vs_serviceability
conflict_axes.description: Hiding a tracker deep resists theft-ring removal and tampering but buys a panel teardown per future service touch and risks burying the antenna; a shallow mount services in minutes but strips easier.
poles: mount shallow for service and antenna
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: shallowest mount meeting the documented risk for that asset class, photo in the record either way; concealment never targets the disclosed workforce

conflict_axes.name: install_throughput_vs_workmanship
conflict_axes.description: Batch-day economics reward speed per unit while the workmanship floor - fusing, dressing, photos - costs exactly the minutes speed wants back.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: the floor is non-negotiable; adjust batch size and windows, and treat over-budget bay times as a planning signal, not a corner to cut

conflict_axes.name: plugin_simplicity_vs_hardwired_permanence
conflict_axes.description: OBD plug-ins install in minutes and self-install by mail, but sit visible, occupy the port and unplug in a second; hardwiring is permanent and tamper-resistant but costs bay time per unit and per-model design work.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: decide per unit class from unplug exposure, port conflicts, connector type and pilot-versus-committed status; OBD choices carry mandatory unplug alerting

conflict_axes.name: ping_rate_vs_battery_budget
conflict_axes.description: Faster asset-tracker pings give fresher positions and quicker recovery but every extra daily fix and cold month draws down a battery meant to last years.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set the sparse baseline from the inventory question the customer actually asked, and spend battery on in-motion and recovery modes rather than on idle-day pings

conflict_axes.name: alert_coverage_vs_alert_fatigue
conflict_axes.description: Every additional alert type promises another caught event, and every one past the fleet's acting capacity trains recipients to ignore the channel entirely.
poles: alert on everything that could matter
alert only where someone will act
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: named recipient and expected action per alert; start few, tune upward from observed events in the co-piloted first weeks

conflict_axes.name: management_visibility_vs_driver_trust
conflict_axes.description: Richer behavior monitoring serves safety and cost management but reads as surveillance to the workforce, and resentment converts directly into unplugs, grievances and turnover.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: monitor what the disclosed policy states and no more, frame uses honestly including the ones that protect drivers, and treat unplug clusters as a trust signal before a discipline signal

conflict_axes.name: config_richness_vs_admin_capacity
conflict_axes.description: Fences, alerts and reports are nearly free to create and each one is maintenance debt against a fleet admin with minutes per day; a rich config the admin abandons is worth less than a thin one they use.
poles: configure what the fleet will maintain
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: every artifact names its consumer; unconsumed config is pruned at the week-one review, not defended

conflict_axes.name: fleet_standardization_vs_per_unit_fit
conflict_axes.description: One device family and one install pattern across the fleet simplifies stock, training and support, but mixed fleets - vans plus tractors plus tilt trailers - genuinely need different families per class.
poles: fit the family per unit class
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: standardize within unit class, never across power-source boundaries; the matrix records the reason so support knows why the fleet carries three families

conflict_axes.name: go_live_speed_vs_verified_handoff
conflict_axes.description: The customer and the sales side want trucks tracking this week; verification, disclosure acknowledgment, training and documentation all sit between install and honest acceptance.
poles: hand off only what is verified, disclosed and documented
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: compress by parallelizing (disclosure and provisioning run before install day), never by dropping gate conditions; an eager customer is walked through the gate, not around it

edge_cases.description: A heavy tractor's diagnostic connector is a 9-pin round deutsch style, not OBD-II, and the shipped plug-in trackers do not fit
edge_cases.trigger: OBD-family devices meet a heavy-truck or older-vehicle connector
edge_cases.mitigation: catch port type at intake; heavy classes get adapter harnesses specified in advance or go hardwired, and the matrix records the connector reason

edge_cases.description: One van's tracker goes offline every Friday afternoon and returns Monday; the device is fine, the driver unplugs it for weekend side work
edge_cases.trigger: a pattern of offline windows correlated with one vehicle's shifts
edge_cases.mitigation: unplug alerting plus the triage human bucket route it to the fleet's management as a policy matter, not a hardware swap; disclosure policy already told drivers unplugging is visible

edge_cases.description: A current-model pickup has no clean switched circuit; the tapped 'ignition' wire wakes at night for software updates, logging ghost trips
edge_cases.trigger: multiplexed vehicle electronics defeat wire-based ignition sensing
edge_cases.mitigation: flip the model's design sheet to voltage-threshold or accelerometer virtual ignition and re-verify ignition events on the first unit before the batch proceeds

edge_cases.description: An asset tracker mounted under a trailer's steel deck passed its bench test but reports no fixes in the field
edge_cases.trigger: a mount position blocks GPS sky view on a metal asset
edge_cases.mitigation: verification at the install location catches it same-day; remount per the sky-view spec and ban the position in the standard

edge_cases.description: Several vehicles are take-home: employees commute in them, so tracking runs through evenings and weekends at their homes
edge_cases.trigger: the parking-pattern question at intake reveals take-home units
edge_cases.mitigation: surface off-hours visibility explicitly in the disclosed policy, flag jurisdictional off-hours monitoring rules for verification, and configure business-hours-scoped views where the platform supports them

edge_cases.description: A retail walk-in wants a tracker installed on a car 'for my spouse - do not tell them'
edge_cases.trigger: a covert-individual tracking request reaches the counter dressed as a normal sale
edge_cases.mitigation: the refusal script runs: no install without owner/authorized-operator standing and disclosure where required; the request is declined and logged

edge_cases.description: The fleet's drivers are unionized and the collective agreement has a monitoring-technology consultation clause nobody mentioned at signing
edge_cases.trigger: union or works-council status surfaces after the deal is signed
edge_cases.mitigation: pause go-live for the consultation step, flag the jurisdiction- and agreement-specific duties for verification, and keep installed units dark until the process clears

edge_cases.description: Trucks running a remote highway lane vanish from the map for hours, then their tracks arrive at once and appear to teleport
edge_cases.trigger: store-and-forward buffering in a known coverage hole
edge_cases.mitigation: the coverage note pre-classifies the lane, admin training explains the artifact before the first occurrence, and triage rules out device fault by the last-contact/last-fix pattern

edge_cases.description: A rental fleet swaps attachments and small assets between carrier machines weekly, and utilization reports start crediting hours to the wrong asset
edge_cases.trigger: asset identity churn breaks the device-to-asset binding
edge_cases.mitigation: trackers bind to the tracked asset itself, not to whatever carries it; the manifest is updated as part of the swap procedure and identity is re-verified after each re-binding

edge_cases.description: Install Saturday opens with a third of the listed vehicles absent - two on overnight jobs, one in the body shop, one sold last month
edge_cases.trigger: the yard on install day does not match the intake vehicle list
edge_cases.mitigation: the fallback plan installs what is present, schedules a sweep window for stragglers, and the sold vehicle triggers a unit-list correction before its device is wasted

edge_cases.description: A van's aftermarket LED bar was tapped into the same circuit as the tracker; its short blows the shared fuse and the tracker dies with it weeks later
edge_cases.trigger: other aftermarket electrical work shares or disturbs the tracker's circuit
edge_cases.mitigation: the standard demands a dedicated fused tap; triage's power bucket plus the tap-point photo find the shared-circuit violation fast and the fix isolates the tracker

edge_cases.description: A fleet owner asks for the trackers to be hidden from his own drivers 'so we catch them at it'
edge_cases.trigger: a concealment request aimed at the workforce rather than at thieves
edge_cases.mitigation: decline the covert framing and convert to a disclosed program: the deterrence the owner wants comes from drivers knowing, and the refusal script explains that a covert employee program is a job this business does not do

workflow.description: Capture the per-unit list with power and port facts, parking pattern, duty cycles, report readers and the owner's target questions
workflow.gate: every unit has type, power, port where relevant and parking notes; every target question names its reader

workflow.action: Pass the lawful-use gate and map regulatory flags
workflow.description: Confirm owner/employer authorization per asset, identify notification duties, refuse covert requests, and list the ELD/HOS and privacy classes flagged verify-locally
workflow.gate: authorization confirmed per asset, no covert scope survives, every flagged class carries a verify-in-jurisdiction note

workflow.description: Map every unit class to OBD, hardwired or asset-tracker family with a written reason
workflow.gate: no unit class unmapped, no family assigned against its power or connector facts

workflow.action: Qualify network coverage per operating area
workflow.description: Verify carrier reality in yards, sites and lanes, note dead zones and buffering behavior, screen for network sunsets
workflow.gate: every operating area has a note; no committed SKU rides a sunset-flagged network in-region

workflow.description: Create groups mirroring the org, fix the naming convention, assign least-privilege roles, verify time zone and business hours
workflow.gate: structure matches intake's org, naming convention written, roles least-privilege, time settings verified

workflow.description: Deliver the plain-language policy, hold the framing session, collect signed acknowledgments, clear any union/works-council consultation
workflow.artifact: signed acknowledgment set and policy on file
workflow.gate: every affected driver acknowledged before their unit goes live; consultation documented or explicitly not applicable

workflow.description: Bench-activate every device, build the pairing manifest binding device to asset and name, print labels, sort boxes per vehicle
workflow.artifact: pairing manifest and labeled staged devices
workflow.gate: all devices reporting on the bench; manifest has no duplicate device, SIM, asset or name entries

workflow.description: Execute per-model designs with fused taps, dressed wiring, no-go-zone clearance, weatherproofing, and pre-close photos
workflow.gate: spot-checked units meet the standard; every record carries mount and tap photos taken before panels closed

workflow.action: Verify every unit in the field
